::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. table.title: Psychometric properties of the Parental Burnout Assessment: Invariance testing and comparative analysis of burnout related symptoms among parents of children with and without complex care needs
table.stopping_rule: As the data for parents of children with CCN is based on data needed for the longitudinal analysis, recruitment was stopped after enough participants had filled in the questionnaire to conduct the longitudinal analysis, as determined by power calculations. In this study, we only use the baseline data. As for the data on parents of children without CCN, only panel members who filled out the first questionnaire during a two-month timespan were invited to fill out the second questionnaire. Similarly, only participants who filled out the second questionnaire were invited to fill out the third questionnaire. For the fourth questionnaire (which included the PBA), only panel members who filled in the third questionnaire were invited. Additionally, if two parents from the same household had filled in the third questionnaire, only one of these was invited to fill out the fourth and last questionnaire. This ensured that each respondent belonged to a different household.

table.research_questions:
Hypothesis 1 (invariance testing): Given that previous studies have suggested that conceptualizations of burnout among parents of children with CCN only partially align with the dimensions for burnout as proposed by the PBA, it remains uncertain whether the PBA captures the experiences of these parents in the same way as it does for parents without children with CCN. Hence, the PBA may not demonstrate full measurement invariance across parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN, which would need to be taken into account for cross-group comparisons. 

Hypothesis 2 (descriptives): To the extent that the PBA can be considered invariant, differences in burnout scores are expected, with parents of children with CCN reporting higher levels of parental burnout than parents of children without CCN. These differences may also occur on different dimensions of the PBA and on item level. 

Hypothesis 3 (examine the associations between socio-demographic characteristics and burnout scores among parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN). Existing literature suggests that socio-demographic characteristics are associated to a limited extent with the development of burnout related thoughts and feelings.

We expect the associations between socio-demographic characteristics and the PBA to differ for parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN. Eight socio-demographic factors will be subjected to analysis: parental age, sex, ethnicity, educational attainment, single parent, minimum and maximum child age. Given the limited and inconsistent evidence in the literature regarding socio-demographic correlates on parental burnout, these analyses were largely exploratory. Except maximum and minimum child age. We expect maximum child age to be related to higher burnout scores among parents of children with CCN, due to the duration of intense caregiving. We expect minimum child age to be related to higher burnout scores among parents of children without CCN, due to the intense caregiving of children below 5 years.   


For some variables, we propose directional hypotheses based on theoretical and empirical grounds: 
 -Parental age: Among parents of children with CCN a positive association is expected, as older parents may have been exposed to stressors for a longer period. 
-Gender: Female gender is expected to be associated with higher burnout, likely due to greater share in caregiving responsibilities, societal expectations, or role strain. 
-Ethnicity: Parents with a migration background may report higher burnout levels due to compounded stressors (e.g., migration-related stress, limited access to informal support networks).
-Child’s age: A positive association may be expected, reflecting longer duration of care-related stress. However, this variable may be statistically confounded by parental age (multicollinearity). 
-Family composition: Single parents are expected to report higher burnout levels, given the greater caregiving and emotional burden.
-Education: A negative association is hypothesized, as higher educational attainment may reflect greater access to material and psychological resources.

For other variables, we refrain from making strong directional predictions due to conceptual ambiguity or limited prior evidence:  
-Occupation: The relationship with burnout is less straightforward. Working may reflect either additional stress (double burden) or reduced care burden (e.g., through formal care support), complicating interpretation. 
-Number of children: The association may depend on birth order (e.g., whether the child with CCN is the firstborn or not) and division of caregiving responsibilities. Therefore, no clear directional hypothesis is formulated.

Based on the assumption that socio-demographic factors further increase the levels of stress of parents of children with CCN, we expect stronger associations between socio-demographic factors and burnout for parents with CCN compared to parents without CCN.

table.data_collection_procedures:
Data on parents of children with CCN (In Kaart)

This study is conducted as part of the project Ouders in Evenwicht (Balanced Parents). The data was collected through In Kaart, a register for people with neurodivergence and/or disabilities and their next of kin in the Netherlands (In Kaart | In Kaart - register voor en door mensen met ontwikkelingsproblemen.). Recruitment of participants was a collaborative effort between the project group of Ouders in Evenwicht and In Kaart. Participants were approached to participate in “a study regarding burnout and resilience among parents of children with complex care needs.”

Recruitment occurred through multiple channels: parental organizations and platforms, Facebook groups for parents of children with various illnesses/ disabilities, patient organizations, conferences for healthcare professionals and parents, and schools. We also used the our project group members' personal networks via platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn. Interest groups, the network of the steering committee members of In Kaart, relevant healthcare institutions (e.g., general practitioners, child health clinics, mental health care services, Municipal Public Health Service, rehabilitation centers) were also instrumental in the recruitment process. Recruitment materials (e-mails, social media messages, and flyers) were prepared in collaboration with experts by experience, ensuring they were relevant and sensitive to the target audience.

Data collection started 5th of September 2022 and ended 30th of June 2023. The data collected for this study was the first measurement wave of ongoing data collections.

Inclusion criteria of parents of children with CCN 

Parents (biological, legal guardians, adoptive, or stepparents) were eligible to participate if they had a child with CCN below 16 years. CCN was defined as “…those who have or are at increased risk of chronic physical, developmental, behavioral, or emotional conditions and who also require health and related services beyond what is typically required by children” (McPherson et al., 1998, p. 138). Parents were also encouraged to participate if there was a suspicion of a diagnosis or if they worried about the health or development of their child, this was to ensure that the study reflected the experiences of a diverse group of parents, making the findings more applicable to a wider group of parents and improving the relevance of the results for similar populations. Furthermore, the age limit of 16 years was chosen due to privacy regulations in the Netherlands, where parents of children aged 16 or above are not allowed to provide information about the child without the child's consent. 

Data for parents of children without CCN (LISS-panel)

The recruitment of participants and data collection were handled by the independent non-profit institute Centerdata using the LISS panel. The LISS panel is a household panel consisting of approximately 7500 panel members from 5,000 households. The panel is based on a probability sample drawn from the population register by Statistics Netherlands (CBS). Through this sample Centerdata tries to create a representative sample of the Dutch population. The members of the panel receive monthly invitations via email to participate in questionnaires. For the data collection such a standard mail was used. 
All LISS data are available for non-commercial purposes through a freely accessible and advanced data archive. Centerdata is an official partner of Tilburg University. Before a household can participate in the LISS panel, they must give informed consent in three different steps. Monthly participants are invited to fill in surveys for which they get compensated (Home - LISS panel).  

The data for this study was collected as part of a bigger data collection effort. This data collection took place from August 2024 to December 2024 through online surveys. Data was collected over four waves. Wave 1 took place in August and September, wave 2 in September and October, wave 3 in October and November, and wave 4 in November and December. Only parents who completed the previous wave were invited to participate in the next wave. For this study, only data from wave 1 and wave 4 will be used, as these waves concern child and family characteristics (wave 1), as well as data on the PBA (wave 4). 

For information on sociodemographic characteristics, we also made use of already collected data (LISS background variables and Core Studies). LISS participants are asked each month to update their background information if needed. The background variables are number of persons in household, relationships between persons in household, gender, age, civil status, level of education, type of household, gross and net monthly income for each person in household, type of accommodation, degree of urbanization of place of residence, migration background. Additionally, LISS panel members are asked to fill out yearly recurring questionnaires on topics such as Work and Income or Family and Household (LISS Core Studies).

Inclusion criteria of parents of children without a CCN

Centerdata was instructed to invite panel members to create the following sample: approximately 500 parents with children aged 0 to 18 years, with at least one child living at home. Within this sample of 500 parents, at least 150 parents had to have a child between 5 to 12 years, with an ideal gender ratio of approximately 50% mothers and 50% fathers within this subsample. For the entire sample, we aimed to obtain a minimum of 100 fathers and 100 mothers. It was not a goal to reach a distribution of 50% mother and 50% fathers for the entire sample. Additionally, these 500 parents participating in all four waves had to be part of different households. The overall sample includes parents of children with and without CNN.

Inclusion criteria for the psychometric analysis

To be able to make accurate comparisons, this study includes parents who have at least one child under the age of 16, either with or without CCN. For accurate comparison, those parents who reported having a child with CCN in the LISS-sample were excluded. Among the group of parents with a child with CCN, the child may or may not live at home, whereas for the group without CCN, the child lives at home. Including parents of children with CCN regardless of whether the child lives at home allows for a more comprehensive understanding of parental burnout across a spectrum of caregiving experiences, as the sense of parental responsibility does not cease when the child does not live at home (Patty et al., 2024a).

table.measured_variables:
The Parental Burnout Assessment

The Dutch translated version of Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA) (Roskam et al., 2018) was used to measure parental burnout. This PBA consists of 23 items, covering four dimensions: ‘emotional exhaustion’ in one's parental role (EE: 9 items; e.g., “I feel completely run down by my role as a parent”), ‘emotional distancing’ (ED: 3 items; e.g. “I’m no longer able to show my child(ren) how much I love them”), contrast with previous parental self (CO: 6 items; e.g., “I’m no longer proud of myself as a parent”), and ‘feelings of being fed up’ (FU: 5 items; e.g., “I can’t take being a parent any more”). Items are rated on a 7-point likert scale ranging from 0 (never) to a few times a year or less (1), once a month or less (2), a few times a month (3), once a week (4), a few times a week (5), every day (6). The total score is the sum of the individual items, a higher score reflects more burnout related thoughts and feelings.

table.statistical_tests:
JASP version 0.18 will be used to conduct the analysis. 

The analysis will be conducted following the steps below: 

Research question 1: To what extent does the PBA demonstrate measurement invariance across parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN?

1. Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omegas will be calculated over the total PBA and the 4 subscales for the total sample and both subgroups (parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN).

2. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) will be conducted for both subgroups, using the Lavaan package (Rossel 2012), to test if the four-dimensional structure is similar across groups and to ensure the measurement model fits well in both subgroups independently using the Diagonally Weighted Least Squared (DWLS) method. The model fit will be evaluated using fit indices: and where needed the model will be adjusted. The fit will be assessed through Comparative Fit index (CFI), Chi-Square Test of Model Fit, Tucker–Lewis index (TLI), Root Mean Square Error Of Approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). These fit indices will also be applied in the invariance analysis (see step 3). 

3. Once the CFA shows good fit* in both subgroups, measurement invariance of the total sample (i.e., across parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN) will be conducted using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA) . The invariance analysis will be conducted in a stepwise manner as outlined below (a-d), with each subsequent step performed only if the model demonstrates an acceptable fit at the preceding level. 

a. Configural invariance will be tested with a MG-CFA with two groups (1 = parents of   children with CCN, 2 = parents of children without CCN). Configural invariance tests if the factor structure – that is, the number of factors and factor loadings patterns - is the same across groups. This is done by not setting any constraints on the parameters (factor loadings, item threshold/ intercepts, residual variance). Good fit indicates that parents with children with CCN and those without conceptualize burnout as measured by the PBA similarly. 

b. Metric (weak) invariance tests whether the factor loadings are equal across the groups. This is done by constraining the factor loadings - i.e., the strength of the relationship with the item and the factor loading- to be equal across the subgroups. A good model fit under metric invariance implies that the strength of the relationship between the items and the underlying factor is the same across groups. The model fit will be evaluated and compared to the configural model using delta Chi-Squares. A good fit means that parents of children with CCN and those without interpret the items in a similar way.  

c. Scalar (strong) invariance tests whether the item intercepts/ thresholds are equal across groups, in addition to equal factor loadings. A good fit indicates that parents of children with CCN and those without who have the same level of burnout are equally likely to choose the same response options on each item.  

d. Residual (strict) invariance will be tested, which tests if factor loadings, item thresholds/ intercepts, and residual variance are equal across groups. Residual invariance indicates that parents of children with CCN and those without have the same amount of measurement error or item-specific variance in their responses. 

Research question 2: Taking the structure of the PBA in both samples into account, what are the differences between these two groups? 

If the factor structure of the PBA is found to be invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level:
An ANOVA will be conducted to examine whether there are statistically significant differences in the PBA total score and subscale scores between the two subgroups. 

If the factor structure of the PBA is found not invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level: 
Include descriptives at the item level for each subgroup to examine the variability across items and identify items that may be less relevant or problematic for the CCN subgroup.

Research question 3: Which sociodemographic characteristics (such as, parental age, gender, education, occupation, ethnicity, child’s age, number of children and family composition) are associated with burnout among parents of children with CCN and parents without children without CCN? 

If the factor structure of the PBA is found to be invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level:
Descriptive statistics will be used to compare both subgroups at the subscale level, to provide insight into the distribution of scores and support the interpretation of the means. Socio-demographic factors related to the differences in burnout scores between both groups will be tested. The aim is to understand which socio-demographic factors are associated with burnout related thoughts and feelings given the differences between the two groups. Moderation analyses will be used to examine between-group differences. 

If the factor structure of the PBA is found not invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level: 
Explore the relationship between socio-demographic characteristics and burnout separately for parents of children with CCN and those without. Within each subgroup, regression analysis will be conducted to investigate which socio-demographic characteristics are associated with burnout scores. Since the PBA is not invariant, the aim will not be to explain group differences, but rather to understand which socio-demographic characteristics are related to burnout within each subgroup independently

*If configural invariance is not achieved (step 2) across the four dimensions of the PBA, an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) will be conducted separately for both groups. This will help determine whether an alternative factor structure may be more appropriate for parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN. The goal is to explore whether different dimensions emerge that may better reflect the underlying structure of parental burnout in each group and potentially show configural invariance across groups. If configural invariance can be achieved following a modified factor structure of the PBA, then invariance testing on that factor structure can continue (steps 3a-d). 

Steps 1-3 will also be conducted among parents of children with CCN and the total sample of LISS (n = 450), hence also including those parents in the LISS sample who have a child with CCN. This will serve as supplementary analysis and will not be part of the scientific publication.

Amendments: 
-JASP version 0.95.4 will be used to conduct the analysis. 

After initial data inspection the following adjustments were made to the data analysis: 
- Treating the PBA outcomes as ordinal resulted in better fit indicies and therefore the decision was made to keep the ordinal nature of the PBA in subsequent analysis. However, inspection of the item endorsement showed a positively skewed distribution, especially among parents of children without CCN. The outermost response categories were rarely endorsed. Therefore, several response categories were collapsed to ensure at least 5 respondents in the outermost categories. As very sparse categories can lead to unstable threshold estimations and convergence issues (e.g., Rutkowski, Svetina & Liaw. 2019).  
- Research question 2: Differences across the four burnout dimensions were examined using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) instead of ANOVA, which accounts for multiple testing and for potential correlations among dimensions.
-Research question 3: Occupation was not included in the analysis due to concerns regarding harmonization and interpretability. Specifically, among parents of children with CCN, employment status was assessed without distinguishing between paid employment and unpaid caregiving activities. This ambiguity is further complicated by the fact that some parents may receive financial compensation for caregiving via persoonsgebonden budget (PGB; a Dutch personal care budget that allows individuals or families to receive funds to organize and pay for care themselves), making it unclear whether they consider themselves in paid employment. Additionally, the cross-sectional nature of the data precludes determining whether unemployment is a consequence of caregiving demands or precedes them (i.e., potential reverse causation). Given these uncertainties, inclusion of occupation would have hindered meaningful interpretation of the results.    
- Research question 3: We used the PROCESS model by Hayes (Hayes 2022; Lüken et al., 2024) for the moderation analysis. 

-Amendment February 2026: 
The approach by Hassanein et al. (2025) and Sorkkila et al. (2020) will be followed for the CFA. Three models will be specified to assess the factor structure of the PBA. CFA will be performed for each model separately in both samples: 
-	M1: theoretical four-factor model will be tested, comprising four correlated latent factors representing the dimensions of the PBA: Emotional Exhaustion (EE; 9 items), Contrast with previous parental self (CO; 6 items), Feelings of being fed up (FU; 5 items), and Emotional distancing (ED; 3 items.
-	M2: a one-factor measurement model, in which a single latent factor was specified to underlie all 23 PBA items. 
-	M3: second-order measurement model, to examine whether the associations among the first-order factors in M1 could be explained by a higher-order factor representing overall parental burnout.
Based on the outcome of the CFA, invariance testing will take place for those models that show good model fit according to the model fit criteria. And the outcomes of the invariance testing will further determine the outcome variable to be used in research questions 2 (comparison of the means) and 3 (associated factors).
table.inference_criteria:
A p-value < .05 will be used to determine statistical significance of the results. Due to multiple testing in research question 3 (Which sociodemographic characteristics are associated with burnout among parents of children with CCN and parents without children without CCN?), the Hochberg correction will be applied to control the error rate. This correction is more sensitive for true effects than the Holms-Bonferroni method, which fits the exploratory character of this research question (Blakesley et al., 2009). Furthermore, following the guideline by Ponterotto & Ruckdesdel (2007) and taking into account the sample size and the number of items, Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s Omega’s will be interpreted as follows. For the PBA dimensions ED, CO, FU, a Cronbach’s alpha of ≥ 0.85 will be considered excellent, 0.8-0.84 good, 0.75-0.79 moderate, 0.7-0.74 fair, and < 0.7 unsatisfactory. For the total PBA score and the EE dimension, a Cronbach’s alpha of ≥ 0.9 will be considered excellent, 0.85-0.89 moderate, 0.8-0.84 fair, < 0.8 unsatisfactory. To determine an acceptable model fit, Chi-Square test needs to be non-significant. CFI and TLI  >.9 are considered acceptable to good and the recommended cut-off value for RMSEA is ≤ .08, with values ≤ .05 indicating a better model fit (van de Schoot, Lugtig & Hox, 2012). SRMR should be ≤ .08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999).

Amendments: 
-Models were compared by computing the differences (Δ) in RMSEA, CFI, and SRMR values between each successive level of measurement invariance. Measurement invariance was supported if the change in the fit indices was small, specifically when ΔRMSEA <.015, ΔCFI <.01, and ΔSRMR <.030 for metric invariance or <.015 for scalar and strict invariance (Chen, 2007; Putnick & Bornstein, 2016). 

Amendment February 2026: 
-For research question 2 (regarding comparisons of mean scores): Effect sizes will be converted to Cohen’s d to facilitate comparisons across findings (Lenhard & Lenhard, 2022). Effect sizes were interpreted using the following thresholds: very small = 0.10, small = 0.20, medium = 0.40, and large = 0.63 (Funder & Ozer, 2019).

Inclusion criteria of parents of children with CCN

Parents (biological, legal guardians, adoptive, or stepparents) were eligible to participate if they had a child with CCN below 16 years. Parents were also encouraged to participate if there was a suspicion of a diagnosis or if they worried about the health or development of their child, this was to ensure that the study reflected the experiences of a diverse group of parents, making the findings more applicable to a wider group of parents and improving the relevance of the results for similar populations. The panel is based on a probability sample drawn from the population register by Statistics Netherlands (CBS). Through this sample Centerdata tries to create a representative sample of the Dutch population. The members of the panel receive monthly invitations via email to participate in questionnaires. For the data collection such a standard mail was used.
All LISS data are available for non-commercial purposes through a freely accessible and advanced data archive. Centerdata is an official partner of Tilburg University. Monthly participants are invited to fill in surveys for which they get compensated (Home - LISS panel).

The data for this study was collected as part of a bigger data collection effort. This data collection took place from August 2024 to December 2024 through online surveys. Data was collected over four waves. Wave 1 took place in August and September, wave 2 in September and October, wave 3 in October and November, and wave 4 in November and December. Only parents who completed the previous wave were invited to participate in the next wave. For this study, only data from wave 1 and wave 4 will be used, as these waves concern child and family characteristics (wave 1), as well as data on the PBA (wave 4).

The analysis will be conducted following the steps below:

Research question 1: To what extent does the PBA demonstrate measurement invariance across parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN?

1. Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omegas will be calculated over the total PBA and the 4 subscales for the total sample and both subgroups (parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN).

2. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) will be conducted for both subgroups, using the Lavaan package (Rossel 2012), to test if the four-dimensional structure is similar across groups and to ensure the measurement model fits well in both subgroups independently using the Diagonally Weighted Least Squared (DWLS) method. The model fit will be evaluated using fit indices: and where needed the model will be adjusted. The fit will be assessed through Comparative Fit index (CFI), Chi-Square Test of Model Fit, Tucker–Lewis index (TLI), Root Mean Square Error Of Approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). These fit indices will also be applied in the invariance analysis (see step 3).

3. Once the CFA shows good fit* in both subgroups, measurement invariance of the total sample (i.e., across parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN) will be conducted using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA) . The invariance analysis will be conducted in a stepwise manner as outlined below (a-d), with each subsequent step performed only if the model demonstrates an acceptable fit at the preceding level.

a. Configural invariance will be tested with a MG-CFA with two groups (1 = parents of children with CCN, 2 = parents of children without CCN). Configural invariance tests if the factor structure – that is, the number of factors and factor loadings patterns - is the same across groups. This is done by not setting any constraints on the parameters (factor loadings, item threshold/ intercepts, residual variance). Good fit indicates that parents with children with CCN and those without conceptualize burnout as measured by the PBA similarly.

b. Metric (weak) invariance tests whether the factor loadings are equal across the groups. This is done by constraining the factor loadings - i.e., the strength of the relationship with the item and the factor loading- to be equal across the subgroups. A good model fit under metric invariance implies that the strength of the relationship between the items and the underlying factor is the same across groups. The model fit will be evaluated and compared to the configural model using delta Chi-Squares. A good fit means that parents of children with CCN and those without interpret the items in a similar way.

c. Scalar (strong) invariance tests whether the item intercepts/ thresholds are equal across groups, in addition to equal factor loadings. A good fit indicates that parents of children with CCN and those without who have the same level of burnout are equally likely to choose the same response options on each item.

d. Residual (strict) invariance will be tested, which tests if factor loadings, item thresholds/ intercepts, and residual variance are equal across groups. Residual invariance indicates that parents of children with CCN and those without have the same amount of measurement error or item-specific variance in their responses.

Research question 2: Taking the structure of the PBA in both samples into account, what are the differences between these two groups?

If the factor structure of the PBA is found to be invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level:
An ANOVA will be conducted to examine whether there are statistically significant differences in the PBA total score and subscale scores between the two subgroups.

If the factor structure of the PBA is found not invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level:
Include descriptives at the item level for each subgroup to examine the variability across items and identify items that may be less relevant or problematic for the CCN subgroup.

Research question 3: Which sociodemographic characteristics (such as, parental age, gender, education, occupation, ethnicity, child’s age, number of children and family composition) are associated with burnout among parents of children with CCN and parents without children without CCN?

If the factor structure of the PBA is found to be invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level:
Descriptive statistics will be used to compare both subgroups at the subscale level, to provide insight into the distribution of scores and support the interpretation of the means. Socio-demographic factors related to the differences in burnout scores between both groups will be tested. The aim is to understand which socio-demographic factors are associated with burnout related thoughts and feelings given the differences between the two groups. Moderation analyses will be used to examine between-group differences.

If the factor structure of the PBA is found not invariant between the two subgroups at least at the configural invariance level:
Explore the relationship between socio-demographic characteristics and burnout separately for parents of children with CCN and those without. Within each subgroup, regression analysis will be conducted to investigate which socio-demographic characteristics are associated with burnout scores. Since the PBA is not invariant, the aim will not be to explain group differences, but rather to understand which socio-demographic characteristics are related to burnout within each subgroup independently

*If configural invariance is not achieved (step 2) across the four dimensions of the PBA, an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) will be conducted separately for both groups. This will help determine whether an alternative factor structure may be more appropriate for parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN. The goal is to explore whether different dimensions emerge that may better reflect the underlying structure of parental burnout in each group and potentially show configural invariance across groups. If configural invariance can be achieved following a modified factor structure of the PBA, then invariance testing on that factor structure can continue (steps 3a-d).

Steps 1-3 will also be conducted among parents of children with CCN and the total sample of LISS (n = 450), hence also including those parents in the LISS sample who have a child with CCN. This will serve as supplementary analysis and will not be part of the scientific publication.

info.title: Running Head: INVARIANCE OF THE PARENTAL BURNOUT ASSESSMENT
keywords: parents of children with complex care needs

text.text: Objective.

This study evaluated the measurement invariance of the Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA) across parents of children with complex care needs (CCN) and parents of children without CCN and studied the difference in burnout scores and their associations with sociodemographic factors.
Design.
The PBA was completed by 337 parents of children with CCN and 329 parents of children without CCN.
A multigroup-confirmatory factor analysis was employed to test measurement invariance.
Group differences in total and subscale scores were examined.

Stepwise regression included sociodemographic variables (parental age, sex, ethnicity, educational attainment, single parent, minimum child age, maximum child age, and the number of children) and parental CCN status with its interaction term as a moderator.
Results.
Scalar invariance was established for a four-factor model and a second-order model of the PBA, indicating that the observed differences in PBA scores reflect true differences.
Parents of children with CCN reported higher PBA scores than parents of children without CCN (d = 1.33, p < .001).
text.formatted: Parents of children with CCN reported higher PBA scores than parents of children without CCN (d = 1.33, p < .001).

text.text: Being a mother of a child with CCN was associated with substantially higher PBA scores compared to being a father.
This difference was smaller among parents of children without CCN.
Other sociodemographic characteristics were not associated with higher scores.
Conclusions.

Findings underscore the heightened vulnerability for parental burnout among parents of children with CCN compared to parents of children without CCN while also providing further evidence for the suitability of the PBA as a research instrument for assessing parental burnout across these caregiving contexts.
While parenting can be deeply rewarding, it also comes with significant challenges, especially for parents of children with complex care needs (CCN).
Children with CCN have a combination of enduring physical, developmental, behavioral, and/or emotional problems and needs, requiring care beyond what is typically required (McPherson et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Children with CCN have a combination of enduring physical, developmental, behavioral, and/or emotional problems and needs, requiring care beyond what is typically required <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McPherson et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Parents of children with CCN face unique demands, such as extensive daily assistance, complex medical tasks, and uncertainty regarding the disability or illness and its progression (Hodapp et al., 2019; Power et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Parents of children with CCN face unique demands, such as extensive daily assistance, complex medical tasks, and uncertainty regarding the disability or illness and its progression <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hodapp et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Power et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The concept of "parental burnout" was introduced in the 1980s to describe how prolonged exposure to parentingrelated stress may have severe long-term psychosocial effects (Procaccini & Kiefaber, 1983).
text.formatted: The concept of "parental burnout" was introduced in the 1980s to describe how prolonged exposure to parentingrelated stress may have severe long-term psychosocial effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Procaccini & Kiefaber, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Parental burnout is often linked to the burden of prolonged caregiving demands without reprieve.
The Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA) has emerged as a preferred questionnaire (Arikan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA) has emerged as a preferred questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arikan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Research on parental burnout has grown rapidly (Mikolajczak et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2024), with several studies comparing burnout levels between parents of children with CCN to those without (for a review see Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Research on parental burnout has grown rapidly <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mikolajczak et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ren et al., 2024)</ref>, with several studies comparing burnout levels between parents of children with CCN to those without (for a review see <ref type="bibr">Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Parents of children with CCN tend to report higher levels of burnout compared to parents of children without CCN, with prevalence estimates ranging from 20-77% for parents of children with CCN (compared to 20-34% among parents of children without CCN).

Several factors may contribute to the wide range in estimates, including the use of diverse instruments for measuring burnout, heterogeneity on sociodemographic factors across populations, and potential differences in the meaning of the construct.

Moreover, some studies suggest that parental burnout may manifests itself differently among parents of children with CCN than those without (Abdoli et al., 2020; Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, some studies suggest that parental burnout may manifests itself differently among parents of children with CCN than those without <ref type="bibr">(Abdoli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the aim of the present study was to examine the measurement invariance of the PBA across parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN.

Taking invariance into account, levels of burnout-related thoughts and feelings between these two groups were compared, and the associations between sociodemographic characteristics and burnout scores explored, given the caregiving context of having a child with CCN or not.
Developed by Roskam et al. (2018), the PBA has demonstrated strong psychometric properties across languages and cultural contexts (Roskam et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Roskam et al. (2018)</ref>, the PBA has demonstrated strong psychometric properties across languages and cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Roskam et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The PBA consists of 23 items and conceptualizes parental burnout through four dimensions: emotional exhaustion in the parental role, emotional distancing from one's child, feelings of being fed up with the parental role, and contrast with previous parental self.

To date, its invariance has been tested across parental education level, gender, and languages (see Aunola et al., 2020; Roskam et al., 2021) both for the four-factor structure and PBA as a higher-order factor, representing overall parental burnout.
text.formatted: To date, its invariance has been tested across parental education level, gender, and languages (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aunola et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Roskam et al., 2021)</ref> both for the four-factor structure and PBA as a higher-order factor, representing overall parental burnout.

text.text: The PBA has also been used in parents of children with CCN (Aviad et al., 2024; Dzielińska et al., 2024; Hassanein et al., 2025; Roskam & Mikolajczak, 2023).
text.formatted: The PBA has also been used in parents of children with CCN <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Aviad et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dzielińska et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hassanein et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roskam & Mikolajczak, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is unknown whether the four-factor structure of the PBA, developed from accounts of burned-out mothers in the general population, manifests in the same way among parents of children with CCN.

Qualitative evidence suggests that, for these parents, burnout stems from the double burden of simultaneously parenting and providing intensive, ongoing care (Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024; Patty et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Qualitative evidence suggests that, for these parents, burnout stems from the double burden of simultaneously parenting and providing intensive, ongoing care <ref type="bibr">(Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Patty et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This experience encompasses substantial physical, emotional, and organizational strain, compounded by the long-term and inescapable nature of caregiving responsibilities (Abdoli et al., 2020; Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This experience encompasses substantial physical, emotional, and organizational strain, compounded by the long-term and inescapable nature of caregiving responsibilities <ref type="bibr">(Abdoli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although the qualitative findings show conceptual overlap with the four dimensions of the PBA, parent's experiences were organized and emphasized somewhat differently.

For example, in the study by Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., (2024) survival mode emerged as a prominent theme in the conceptualization of burnout among parents of children with CCN, reflecting the need to continue functioning despite exhaustion and distancing, due to the ongoing caregiving responsibilities.
text.formatted: For example, in the study by <ref type="bibr">Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., (2024)</ref> survival mode emerged as a prominent theme in the conceptualization of burnout among parents of children with CCN, reflecting the need to continue functioning despite exhaustion and distancing, due to the ongoing caregiving responsibilities.

text.text: Although survival mode is not considered a dimension of the PBA, it illustrates how the intensive and ongoing caregiving context may shape how some aspects of burnout are experienced.

Hence, this context adds to the possibility that, despite some conceptual overlap, the PBA may not capture these experiences in the same way across parents of children with CCN and those without children with CCN.
On top of this, conceptual overlap by itself does not necessarily imply measurement invariance.

Even when the same dimensions are present across groups, individual items may relate differently to the dimensions. (Abdoli et al., 2020; Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024)In the light these considerations, we suggest that while the PBA captures important facets of parental burnout, its structure and content may only partially represent the lived experiences of parents of children with CCN, potentially limiting its applicability in this population.

text.text: This aligns with the findings from a meta-analysis which found that the effect of sociodemographic factors on parental burnout may vary depending on the caregiving context, with no consistent associations observed for factors such as age, gender, education, or single parenthood (Mikolajczak et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This aligns with the findings from a meta-analysis which found that the effect of sociodemographic factors on parental burnout may vary depending on the caregiving context, with no consistent associations observed for factors such as age, gender, education, or single parenthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mikolajczak et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: To date, only one study has investigated the associations between sociodemographic factors and parental burnout among parents with children with CCN compared to parents without children with CCN.

Using the Parental Burnout Inventory (PBI; Roskam et al., 2018), Gérain and Zech (2018) found no significant associations between parental burnout and sociodemographic variablesincluding parental age, sex, education level, working part time, single parenting, and the number of children -when comparing parents of children with CCN to those without.
text.formatted: Using the Parental Burnout Inventory (PBI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Roskam et al., 2018)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gérain and Zech (2018)</ref> found no significant associations between parental burnout and sociodemographic variablesincluding parental age, sex, education level, working part time, single parenting, and the number of children -when comparing parents of children with CCN to those without.

text.text: Consequently, if measurement invariance is established, we can appropriately assess the associations between sociodemographic factors and parental burnout given the caregiving context of parenting a child with CCN or not, as it ensures that the comparison is not confounded by potential group differences in the interpretation of the PBA.

In sum, meaningful comparisons between parents with and without a child with CCN depend on whether the PBA can be considered invariant -that is, the degree to which the PBA measures the same construct in the same way across these two groups.

When invariance cannot be established, that is when the PBA does not measure the concept of parental burnout in the same way across the two groups, caution is needed when drawing conclusions about group differences.

Once invariance has been established, it becomes relevant to examine whether the caregiving context of having a child with CCN or not also affects the associations between sociodemographic factors and parental burnout.

Clarifying this helps detangle the unique psychological impact of intense caregiving from broader structural or contextual factors, thereby informing the design of more targeted support strategies and policy interventions aimed at reducing parental burnout.

The primary aim of this paper is to investigate measurement invariance of the PBA across parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN and the secondary aim is to investigate the differences in the PBA scores and the association with sociodemographic characteristics in both groups, given the caregiving context of having a child with CCN or not.

First, we hypothesize that PBA may demonstrate only partial measurement invariance across parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN, based on the differences in the emphasis of certain aspects of burnout, despite substantial conceptual overlap with the PBA from the qualitative accounts of parents (Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024). text.text: Third, we expect the associations between sociodemographic characteristics and the PBA to differ for parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN.
Eight sociodemographic factors will be subjected to analysis: parental age, sex, ethnicity, educational attainment, single parent, minimum and maximum child age.
Considering the limited and inconsistent evidence in the literature regarding sociodemographic correlates on parental burnout, these analyses were largely exploratory.

The exception was our hypothesis regarding child age, for which differential associations with parental burnout were expected depending on both the age of the youngest and the age of the oldest child and the caregiving context (i.e., having a child with CCN or not).
Among parents in general, having a child younger than 5 years was associated with higher burnout scores, likely due to caregiving demands being at their peak (Mikolajczak et al., 2018).

text.text: In contrast, among parents of children with a CCN, a longer caregiving history may be associated with elevated burnoutrelated thoughts and feelings.
Accordingly, we expect that, in this group, having an older child will be associated with higher levels of parental burnout.
This assumption reflects the cumulative burden of long-term caregiving and has not yet been explored in the parental burnout literature.

The data were collected online through In Kaart, a Dutch register for people with neurodivergence and/or disabilities and their families (InKaart.org).
In Kaart is a noncommercial research register established to facilitate scientific research.

Ethical approval was obtained from the Scientific and Ethical Review Board of the Faculty of Behavioural and Movement Sciences of the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (registration number: VCWE-2022-103).

Participants were recruited by the project group and In Kaart through parental organizations, social media, patient organizations, conferences, schools, healthcare institutions, and the personal networks of project members.
Participation was voluntary, and no financial compensation was provided.
Interested parents first registered to participate in the study, after which each participant received a unique code and individual link to access the online questionnaire.
The questionnaire was therefore not accessible through an open survey link.
Recruitment materials were co-developed with experts by experience to ensure sensitivity and relevance.
Data collection took place between September 5, 2022, and June 30, 2023.
Participants were approached to participate in "a study regarding burnout and resilience among parents of children with complex care needs".
Parents were invited to participate if they had a child with CCN, suspected a diagnosis, or were concerned about their child's health or development.

Eligibility was based on parental reports and was not independently verified through medical records or clinical assessment, as this could exclude families of children with substantial care needs who were still undergoing diagnostic assessment.

As an additional indication of the care needs within the sample, among the parents included in the PBA analyses who provided information on formal care and/ or support (n = 303), 80% (n = 241) reported that their child received formal care and/ or support.

This broad recruitment strategy among parents of children with CCN was chosen to help capture the heterogeneity in children's conditions and care needs and to avoid restricting the sample to a specific diagnosis or clinical population, as is commonly done in research on burnout among parents of children with CCN (Mroskova et al., 2020; Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024).

text.text: Parents (biological, legal guardians, adoptive, or stepparents) were eligible to participate if they had a child with CCN below 16 years.

CCN was defined as "…those who have or are at increased risk of chronic physical, developmental, behavioral, or emotional conditions and who also require health and related services beyond what is typically required by children" (McPherson et al., 1998, p. 138).
text.formatted: CCN was defined as "…those who have or are at increased risk of chronic physical, developmental, behavioral, or emotional conditions and who also require health and related services beyond what is typically required by children" <ref type="bibr">(McPherson et al., 1998, p. 138)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the age limit of 16 years was chosen due to privacy regulations in the Netherlands, where parents of children aged 16 or above are not allowed to provide information about the child without the child's consent.

text.text: Within this sample of 500 parents, at least 150 parents had to have a child between 5 to 12 years, with an ideal gender ratio of approximately 50% mothers and 50% fathers within this subsample.
For the entire sample, no ideal gender ratio was defined, instead the aim was a minimum of 100 fathers and 100 mothers.
Additionally, parents had to be part of different households.
The original comparison sample provided by Centerdata also included parents who reported having a child with CCN.
In the present study, these parents were excluded from the comparison sample to create a comparison group consisting of parents of children without CCN.
Data for parents of children with CCN were collected through Qualtrics and imported into IBM SPSS statistical software program (Version 29.0).
Data for parents of children without CCN were obtained from Centerdata in a CSV and SPSS file.
The data harmonization and exploration of the data occurred in SPSS.
The Dutch translation of the PBA (Roskam et al., 2018 (Roskam et al., , 2021) ) was used to measure parental burnout.
text.formatted: The Dutch translation of the PBA <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Roskam et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Roskam et al., , 2021) )</ref> was used to measure parental burnout.

text.text: The PBA consists of 23 items, covering four dimensions: "emotional exhaustion" in one's parental role (EE: 9 items; e.g., "I feel completely run down by my role as a parent"), "emotional distancing" (ED: 3 items; e.g.

"I'm no longer able to show my child(ren) how much I love them"), "contrast with previous parental self" (CO: 6 items; e.g., "I'm no longer proud of myself as a parent"), and "feelings of being fed up" (FU: 5 items; e.g., "I can't take being a parent any more").

Items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (never) to a few times a year or less (2), once a month or less (3), a few times a month (4), once a week (5), a few times a week (6), every day (7).
The total score is the sum of the individual items; a higher score indicates more burnout related thoughts and feelings.
The total score is commonly used as an outcome measure within research on parental burnout (see e.g., Bian et al., 2025; Dzielińska et al., 2024; Hassanein et al., 2025).

text.text: A range of sociodemographic characteristics was collected, including parental (age, sex, education level, single-parent status and ethnicity), child (age, living situation, type of CCN), and family characteristics (number of children).
Sociodemographic variables were harmonized across the two datasets.

For harmonization of the data and to describe the samples, the following response categories were created: parental sex was recoded into female = 1, male = 0; parent education level was classified as0 = none,1 = low (primary education or prevocational secondary school),2 = middle (higher secondary education/preparatory university education or intermediate vocational education), and3 = high (college or university); ethnicity, which was based on what ethnical group the respondent felt they belonged to and was coded as0 = Dutch and1 = non-Dutch or bi-ethnic (i.e., Dutch in combination with other ethnicity); and single parent was coded as0 = not single and1 = single parent.
To test the associations of sociodemographic characteristics with burnout, education was recoded to ensure sufficient respondents per response category.

Categories were merged into secondary/ vocational education = 0 (encompassing primary education, pre-vocational secondary school, higher secondary education/preparatory university education or intermediate vocational education) and higher education = 1 (encompassing college or university degree).

For the child with CCN the following information was obtained: age; living situation of the child categorized as "at home", "not at home", "partially at home"; the presence of behavioral problems; and type of CCN.

For the type of CCN, parents could choose one or more of the following predefined response options: chronic/ serious illness; behavioral, emotional, or learning disorder; motor or sensory disability/ impairment; intellectual disability; or other.

text.text: A total of n = 51 parents engaged in straight-lining, with the majority of the respondents being parents of children without CCN (n = 47).

As parents of children without CCN received financial compensation (five euros per wave) and as approximately half of these parents belonged to the fastest 15% of the group who filled in the questionnaire, these respondents were excluded from the subsequent analyses.
This resulted in a total sample of n = 666 parents.

This approach is consistent with Curran (2016), who recommends combining straight-lining patterns with response times as an initial strategy for identifying and excluding potentially careless respondents.

text.text: Invariance Testing.
First, we investigated the number of missing values for the PBA.
We found a small number of missing values (n = 3; participants who discontinued the PBA midway).
Therefore, a listwise deletion method was applied to handle missing data (Shi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Therefore, a listwise deletion method was applied to handle missing data <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Shi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the PBA was analyzed to determine whether it should be considered as ordinal or interval.
Third, following the approach by Aunola et al. (2020) and Hassanein et al. (2025), three models were specified to assess the factor structure of the PBA.
text.formatted: Third, following the approach by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aunola et al. (2020)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hassanein et al. (2025)</ref>, three models were specified to assess the factor structure of the PBA.

text.text: Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was performed for each model separately in both samples.

First, a theoretical four-factor model (M1) was tested, comprising four correlated latent factors representing the dimensions of the PBA: emotional exhaustion (EE; 9 items), contrast with previous parental self (CO; 6 items), feelings of being fed up (FU; 5 items), and emotional distancing (ED; 3 items).
Second, a one-factor measurement model (M2) was examined, in which a single latent factor was specified to underlie all 23 PBA items.

Third, a second-order measurement model (M3) was assessed, to examine whether the associations among the first-order factors in M1 could be explained by a higher-order factor representing overall parental burnout (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Third, a second-order measurement model (M3) was assessed, to examine whether the associations among the first-order factors in M1 could be explained by a higher-order factor representing overall parental burnout (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">1</ref>).

text.text: Model fit was evaluated to determine whether the model should be retained for subsequent invariance testing, using multiple indices: Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) values greater than .90 were considered indicative of acceptable fit and values > .95 indicative of good fit; Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) values of ≤ .08 indicated acceptable fit, with values ≤ .05 reflecting a better fit (van de Schoot et al., 2012); and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) values ≤ .08 were considered acceptable and < .05 good fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999).

text.text: Next, we ran a multi-group confirmatory factor analysis to assess measurement invariance across parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN.

Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis was conducted in a stepwise manner as proposed by Leitgöb et al. (2023), with each subsequent step undertaken only if the model demonstrated an acceptable fit at the preceding level and changes in the model fit indices.
text.formatted: Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis was conducted in a stepwise manner as proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Leitgöb et al. (2023)</ref>, with each subsequent step undertaken only if the model demonstrated an acceptable fit at the preceding level and changes in the model fit indices.

text.text: We began with (1) configural invariance, examining whether the four-factor structure -specifically, the number of factors and the pattern of factor loadings -was consistent across groups.
At this stage, no equality constraints were imposed on the parameters (factor loadings, item threshold/ intercepts, residual variance).
A good model fit under configural invariance implies that both groups conceptualize the construct in a similar manner.
Then, we assessed (2) metric invariance, testing whether the factor loadings were equal across the groups.
This was done by constraining the factor loadings -that is, the strength of the relation with the item and the factor loading-to be equal across the subgroups.
A good model fit under metric invariance implies that the strength of the relation between the items and the underlying factor is the same across groups.
Next, we assessed (3) scalar invariance, testing whether the item intercepts/ thresholds were equal across groups, in addition to equal factor loadings.

A good fit under scalar invariance indicates that parents of children with CCN and those without CCN who have the same level of burnout were equally likely to choose the same response options on each item.
Attaining scalar invariance is a prerequisite for comparing mean scores across groups.

Finally, we tested (4) strict (residual) invariance across the groups, by additionally constraining the residual variances of the items to be equal, testing whether the amount of measurement error was consistent across the two groups, implying that any remaining differences in observed scores reflected true differences in parental burnout rather than differences in response reliability or measurement precision.
At each step of the invariance testing, we assessed whether the fit of the more constrained model showed any meaningful deterioration by examining changes in the RMSEA, CFI, and SRMR.
Models were compared by computing the differences (Δ) in RMSEA, CFI, and SRMR values between each successive level of measurement invariance.

Measurement invariance was supported if the change in the fit indices was small, specifically when ΔRMSEA <.015, ΔCFI <.01, and ΔSRMR <.03 for metric invariance or <.015 for scalar and strict invariance (Chen, 2007; Putnick & Bornstein, 2016).

text.text: Invariance testing was also conducted across parents of children with CCN and parents in general (i.e., including those parents who had indicated that their child has some form of CCN within the LISS panel) (see Supplement 1).
Internal consistency of the PBA was analyzed in both samples separately for PBA total score and per dimension, using Cronbach's alpha (α) and McDonald's omegas (ω).

Scales with more items tend to yield higher reliability estimates; therefore, stricter benchmarks were used for the EE dimension (9 items) and for the total PBA score (23 items), compared with the shorter ED, CO, and FU subscales (Pontekotto & Ruckdeschel, 2007).

text.text: The distribution of the burnout scores was assessed using Shapiro-Wilks test and Q-Q plots to determine whether normality assumptions were met.
Differences in the overall PBA score between groups were examined using an independent sample t-test.
In case of potential deviations from normality, the Mann-Whitney U test, a nonparametric alternative to the independent-samples t-test was used.
Differences across the four burnout dimensions were examined using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), which accounts for multiple testing and for potential correlations among dimensions.
If the MANOVA indicated significant overall group differences, univariate analyses were planned for each dimension to identify specific effects.
Statistical significance was set at p < .05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was set at p < .05.

text.text: The effect sizes were converted into Cohen's d to facilitate comparisons across findings.
Effect sizes were interpreted using the following thresholds: very small = 0.10, small = 0.20, medium = 0.40, and large = 0.63 (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Lenhard & Lenhard, 2022).
text.formatted: Effect sizes were interpreted using the following thresholds: very small = 0.10, small = 0.20, medium = 0.40, and large = 0.63 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Funder & Ozer, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lenhard & Lenhard, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Eight sociodemographic variables (parental age, sex, ethnicity, educational attainment, single parent, minimum child age, maximum child age, and the number of children) were examined as predictors in separate moderation analyses.
Both youngest and oldest child age were included to capture potential differences related to caregiving demands and duration across having a child with CCN or not.
To compare the effect of child age for both parents with and without a child with CCN, the minimum and maximum age was used.
This variable was not related to the child with CCN.
Accounting for minimum as well as maximum child age offered a conservative proxy for early caregiving demands and for the cumulative duration of caregiving responsibilities.
A stepwise regression was conducted for each sociodemographic variable with the total PBA score as dependent variable.
In the first step, the sociodemographic variable of interest was entered.
In the second step, the dichotomous variable indicating whether the parent has a child with CCN or not (moderator) was added together with the interaction term.
In case the hierarchical model showed the presence of an interaction effect, this interaction effect was scrutinized using the JASP PROCESS module (A. F. Hayes, 2022; Lüken et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In case the hierarchical model showed the presence of an interaction effect, this interaction effect was scrutinized using the JASP PROCESS module <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(A. F. Hayes, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lüken et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: All regression models were estimated using 1,000 bootstrap samples to generate bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals.
All continuous variables were mean-centered to facilitate meaningful interpretation of the regression coefficients (Aiken & West, 1991) as part of the PROCESS module (Hayes, 2025).

text.text: Using semPOWER by Moshagen and Bader (2024), a post hoc analysis was conducted for CFA.

Assuming a RMSEA of .08, with α = .05, df = 224, and n = 328 (the smallest group -parents of children without CCN), the analyses indicated very high statistical power (1 -β = .999) to detect model misfit.

We also ran a sensitivity power analysis to estimate the smallest detectable effect sizes for comparisons of PBA total scores, subdimensions, and the effects of sociodemographic characteristics on PBA.

For differences in PBA total scores between parents of children without CCN (n = 328) and parents of children with CCN (n = 335), a sensitivity analysis for an independent-samples t test in G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007 (Faul et al., , 2009) ) with α = .05 and power = .80 indicated a minimum detectable effect size of d = .22.

text.text: For group differences across the four PBA subdimensions, a sensitivity analysis for a MANOVA with two groups and four dependent variables (α = .05, power = .80, N = 663) indicated a minimum detectable multivariate effect size of f²(V) = .02.

Finally, for the effect of sociodemographic predictors on PBA total scores, a sensitivity analysis using an F test for linear multiple regression (R² increase) with three predictors (α = .05, power = .80, N = 663) indicated a minimum detectable effect size of f² = .02.

These analyses demonstrate that the study was sufficiently powered to detect small effects for the research question regarding the differences in mean scores and the research question regarding the effect of socio-demographics on parental burnout.

text.text: Consequently, the ordinal specification of the PBA was retained and therefore model parameters were estimated using the Weighted Least Squares Mean and Variance adjusted (WLSMV) estimator.

However, due to the sparse responses in the extreme categories of the PBA, response categories were collapsed to ensure a minimum of five responses in the outermost response categories to facilitate CFA analysis.

Very sparse categories can complicate threshold estimation for ordinal data, in particular when some categories have no counts or very low counts, making threshold constraints difficult to estimate (Rutkowski et al., 2019).

The four-factor structure of the PBA demonstrated acceptable fit in both groups.

text.text: Modification indices consistently identified residual covariances between item pairs PBA17-PBA18 and PBA1-PBA3 as potential sources of misfit.

Allowing covariance between PBA1 and PBA3 led to a modest improvement in SRMR among parents without CCN but did not improve fit in the CCN group and none of the suggested modifications substantially reduced RMSEA.
Given the limited improvement and lack of strong theoretical justification, no post hoc modifications were retained.
Overall, the one-factor model demonstrated inferior fit compared to the multidimensional alternatives.
The second-order factor model, in which the four first-order factors from M1 loaded onto a higher-order factor -parental burnout -demonstrated comparable fit to the four-factor model (M1).
Among parents of children without CCN the model yielded χ²(226) = 727, p < .001, CFI = .948, TLI = .941, RMSEA = .082, and SRMR = .072.

text.text: As with M1, RMSEA values were elevated, particularly in the CCN group.
Modification indices again suggested different adjustments across groups.
Specifically, among parents of children without CCN, residual covariance was suggested between item pair PBA1-PBA3, which are related to the exhaustion dimension.
Among parents of children with CCN, however, residual covariance was suggested between item pairs PBA17-PBA18 and PBA5-PBA13, which are related to the contrast dimension.
Since these suggestions were not consistent across groups, it was decided to retain the model without modifications.

The second-order structure (M3) showed overall fit that was comparable to, and in some respects slightly better than, the first-order four-factor model (M1), while providing a more straightforward representation of parental burnout as a higher-order construct.
Given the superior performance of M1 and M3, subsequent invariance testing focused exclusively on these two models.

text.text: Configural invariance was mostly supported, with acceptable fit despite RMSEA slightly above the conventional threshold (.093), indicating that parents of children with and without CCN conceptualize burnout similarly.
Metric invariance was supported, suggesting factor loadings were equivalent and items were interpreted similarly across groups.
Scalar invariance was also supported, indicating that item intercepts were comparable and allowing for valid comparisons of latent mean scores.
The fit indices did not change between scalar and strict invariance.

Finally, a substantial decline in fit was observed for structural invariance, indicating that the pattern of the relations among the factors differed across parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN.
The second order model showed the same patterns as observed in M1.

Configural through scalar invariance was supported, with slightly elevated RMSEA at each step (ranging from .092 to .086), indicating overall acceptable fit and largely consistent model structure across groups.

Supporting that the first-order factors (i.e. dimensions) collectively reflect an overarching second-order factor -parental burnout -and because scalar invariance was established, the overall PBA score means can be meaningfully compared across groups.

However, structural invariance was not supported, indicating that although the PBA measures burnout consistently across both groups, the way that the factors relate to each other differed between parents of children with CCN and parents of children without children with CCN.

Excellent internal consistency was found for all dimensions for both groups, except for t FU, which showed good rather than excellent reliability among parents without a child with CCN and ED, which showed only fair reliability in both groups (see Table 5).

text.text: Follow up univariate tests showed that parents of children with CCN had significantly higher mean scores on all PBA subdimensions.
Furthermore, large effect sizes were observed for group differences on the dimensions of emotional exhaustion, contrast with previous parental self, and feelings of being fed-up.
Medium effect size was observed for differences on the dimension of emotional distancing.
