text.text: In addition, the association between parental sex and total PBA score was significantly moderated by having a child with CCN.
The difference in outcomes between fathers and mothers was larger among parents of children with CCN than parents of children without CCN.
Specifically, mothers of children with CCN scored significantly higher on the PBA than fathers (B = 14.93, SE = 4.08, 95% CI [6.46, 23.14], p = .002).

No other interaction effects were significant, indicating that the associations between sociodemographic factors and parental burnout did not statistically differ between parents with and without children with CCN.
In addition, in all analyses the dichotomous group variable was significantly related to the PBA, also after controlling for sociodemographic variables.

This study evaluated the measurement invariance of the Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA) across parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN, compared burnout scores between these groups, and explored how sociodemographic characteristics related to parental burnout within each parenting context.

The PBA demonstrated scalar invariance across parents with and without children with CCN for both the theoretically proposed four-factor structure (M1) and the second-order structure (M3), in which the first-order latent variables (i.e. dimensions) were accounted for by the overarching factor, parental burnout.

Parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN therefore tended to interpret the items of the PBA similarly and to attach similar value to differences in strength of parental burnout.

Speaking to differences in parental burnout, parents of children with CCN reported higher PBA total scores and per dimension compared to parents of children without CCN, with moderate to large effect sizes.

Regarding sociodemographic characteristics, the most consistent predictor across all models was group membership: being a parent of a child with CCN explained substantially more variance in the total PBA score than any sociodemographic characteristic.
Furthermore, parental sex and the number of children were also significantly associated with parental burnout.
However, only the association between parental sex and total PBA score was significantly moderated by being a parent of a child with CCN or not.

Specifically, being a mother of child with CCN was associated with substantially higher PBA scores compared to being a father of a child with CCN, this difference was smaller among parents of children without CCN.

While qualitative research has suggested that the lived experience of parental burnout may manifest itself differently in parents of children with CCN -often involving long-term stress from intense caregiving tasks such as, administrative burden, and coordination of social and health care (Abdoli et al., 2020; Patty et al., 2025) -our findings indicate that the core construct of parental burnout as operationalized by the subscales of the PBA has comparable meaning across these two care contexts.
text.formatted: While qualitative research has suggested that the lived experience of parental burnout may manifest itself differently in parents of children with CCN -often involving long-term stress from intense caregiving tasks such as, administrative burden, and coordination of social and health care <ref type="bibr">(Abdoli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Patty et al., 2025)</ref> -our findings indicate that the core construct of parental burnout as operationalized by the subscales of the PBA has comparable meaning across these two care contexts.

text.text: Still, it is plausible that the drivers of burnout differ in intensity or impact.
This might not be surprising as the parenting context is always present, also for parents of children with CCN even if these parents engage in tasks beyond normative parenting.
As such, our results support the use of the PBA in research when interested in burnout within the parenting domain.
Clear and substantial differences between mean scores of the PBA among parents of children with CCN and parents of children without CCN were found.
Parents of children with CCN reported significantly higher total PBA scores and higher scores across all dimensions.

This aligns with prior research demonstrating higher burnout scores among parents of children with CCN compared to parents without children with CCN (e.g., Lindahl Norberg et al., 2014; Lindström et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This aligns with prior research demonstrating higher burnout scores among parents of children with CCN compared to parents without children with <ref type="bibr">CCN (e.g., Lindahl Norberg et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lindström et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The present study extends these findings by showing that such differences are also observed when parental burnout is assessed with the PBA, an instrument specifically developed to capture burnout within the parenting role and for which initial evidence of validity has been established.
Together, our findings further support the validity of using the PBA for comparing burnout between parents of children with CCN and without.
However, although the results of the invariance analyses allow the interpretation of mean scores across groups, some caution is warranted.

First, the strict invariance model was not considered invariant and its model parameters were similar to the scalar results, indicating that changes from scalar into strict invariance might not have been applied by the software (Tse et al., 2024).
text.formatted: First, the strict invariance model was not considered invariant and its model parameters were similar to the scalar results, indicating that changes from scalar into strict invariance might not have been applied by the software <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Tse et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Second, some studies argue that strict invariance is necessary in order to compare mean scores when using ordinal data (Tse et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Second, some studies argue that strict invariance is necessary in order to compare mean scores when using ordinal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Tse et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our results indicated a good fit under scalar invariance meaning the four-factor structure of the PBA was consistent across groups, as were the factor loadings and item thresholds, which is consistent with several studies arguing that scalar invariance is sufficient when comparing mean scores among ordinal data (see e.g., Putnick & Bornstein, 2016; Svetina et al., 2020).

text.text: As for the associations with socio-demographics, the most consistent predictor across all models was group membership: being a parent of a child with CCN explained substantially more variance in the total PBA score than any sociodemographic characteristic.
This pattern mirrors previous findings suggesting that being a parent of a child with CCN is associated with parental burnout (e.g., Roskam & Mikolajczak, 2023).
text.formatted: This pattern mirrors previous findings suggesting that being a parent of a child with CCN is associated with parental burnout (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Roskam & Mikolajczak, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, parental sex also showed an association with parental burnout.
Mothers exhibited higher PBA scores than fathers, and this difference was significantly amplified among parents of children with CCN.

The association of being a mother and thereby having a higher parental burnout score is in line with previous research across both populations (e.g., Hassanein et al., 2025; Lin & Szczygieł, 2022; Lindström et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The association of being a mother and thereby having a higher parental burnout score is in line with previous research across both populations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hassanein et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lin & Szczygieł, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lindström et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Mothers often assume disproportionate shares of both routine parenting and (specialized) caregiving compared to fathers.

Furthermore, although the number of children was initially associated with higher burnout, this effect disappeared once being a parent of a child with CCN or not was considered, again highlighting the dominance of caregiving context above sociodemographic factors in explaining parental burnout.

Despite evidence from the general parent population indicating that having young children (<5 years) is associated with higher burnout related thoughts and feelings (Mikolajczak et al., 2018), our findings did not support this association, as minimum child age was not associated with parental burnout.
text.formatted: Despite evidence from the general parent population indicating that having young children (<5 years) is associated with higher burnout related thoughts and feelings <ref type="bibr">(Mikolajczak et al., 2018)</ref>, our findings did not support this association, as minimum child age was not associated with parental burnout.

text.text: An explanation, consistent with the broader parental burnout literature, is that parental burnout reflects the accumulation of ongoing demands over time rather than age-specific caregiving demands.

From this perspective, burnout-related thoughts and feelings emerge when pressures persist without sufficient opportunities for recovery (Mikolajczak & Roskam, 2018), rendering minimum child age a less salient predictor of parental burnout.
text.formatted: From this perspective, burnout-related thoughts and feelings emerge when pressures persist without sufficient opportunities for recovery <ref type="bibr">(Mikolajczak & Roskam, 2018)</ref>, rendering minimum child age a less salient predictor of parental burnout.

text.text: In line with this reasoning, we also hypothesized that maximum child age -particularly among parents of children with CCN -would be associated with higher burnout levels, a proxy reflecting the length of engagement in caregiving.
This hypothesis was also not supported.

One possible explanation is that maximum child age was derived from all children in the household rather than specifically the child with CCN, and that children older than 15 years were excluded due to privacy regulations in the Netherlands.

Because caregiving and parenting responsibilities for children with CCN often extend into late adolescence and adulthood, future studies should include older children to more accurately capture the potential compound effect of caregiving duration.

In addition, longitudinal designs are needed to examine how burnout develops and changes within parents over time, as such designs are better suited to capture cumulative and nonlinear processes than cross-sectional comparisons.

First, although scalar invariance across groups was established, the sparse distribution of responses for most items necessitated collapsing response categories for 22 of the 23 items; this was required to ensure a sufficient number of responses per category for model estimation.

Research in single group models has shown that in case of low cell frequencies, collapsing response categories introduces less bias in model estimates compared to treating the data as continuous (DiStefano et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Research in single group models has shown that in case of low cell frequencies, collapsing response categories introduces less bias in model estimates compared to treating the data as continuous <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(DiStefano et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Liu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While this approach enabled model convergence and stable parameter estimates, it reduced the granularity of the original response scale.
Notably, item thresholds of the two groups could not be compared across groups for the upper response categories of the scale.

Therefore, category collapsing might have resulted in an overestimation of the level of invariance and may have blurred meaningful differences in the interpretation of the highest response categories for parents of children with CCN versus parents of children without CCN (Rutkowski et al., 2019). .
text.formatted: Therefore, category collapsing might have resulted in an overestimation of the level of invariance and may have blurred meaningful differences in the interpretation of the highest response categories for parents of children with CCN versus parents of children without CCN <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Rutkowski et al., 2019)</ref>. .

text.text: Consequently, the invariance results should be interpreted with caution, and future studies should examine whether larger samples allow for full-scale invariance testing without collapsing response categories.
Second, the cross-sectional design restricts causal inference regarding the effect of sociodemographic characteristics on parental burnout.
Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to understand social-ecological factors that might contribute to or reduce parental burnout.
Third, both samples had overrepresentation by highly educated parents and the sample of parents of children with CCN predominantly consisted of mothers of Dutch descent.

This limits the broader generalizability of our findings and highlights the need for recruitment approaches that facilitate greater participation of fathers and parents from more diverse educational and cultural backgrounds.

Importantly sensitivity analysis restricted to mothers only yielded measurement invariance consistent with the findings of the primary sample including also fathers, suggesting that unequal gender composition did not account for the observed measurement invariance results.
Nevertheless, further research into more genderbalanced and diverse samples is warranted.

Fourth, recruitment procedures differed across samples: parents of children with CCN were recruited using materials that explicitly mentioned burnout, which may have created a self-selection bias by attracting parents who resonated with the term, potentially inflating burnout levels in this group.
On the other hand, the study recruitment also mentioned resilience, which may have attracted parents with different experiences.
Parents of children without CCN received financial compensation, which may have increased the risk of insufficient-effort responding.

Although straight-liners were excluded to enhance data quality, we acknowledge that identical response patterns do not necessarily indicate careless responding and that some valid responses may therefore have been excluded.

Future studies should employ more harmonized recruitment strategies that avoid burnout-related terminology and minimize financial incentives to reduce potential biases and enhance comparability across groups.
Fifth, online participation in itself can be selective, with some groups more likely to participate than others (Hargittai & Karaoglu, 2018).
text.formatted: Fifth, online participation in itself can be selective, with some groups more likely to participate than others <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hargittai & Karaoglu, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Parents connected to organizations involved in recruitment or more inclined to participate in online research may therefore have been more likely to participate in this study Although the sample of parents without CCN was based on probability sampling, participation was also subject to nonresponse and study-specific sampling.
Consequently, neither sample should be considered fully representative of its respective parent population.

Considering the differences in recruitment and participation between the two samples, we cannot fully exclude the possibility that the recruitment and data-collection context contributed to differences between the samples (Schnell & Klingwort, 2024).

text.text: Although the PBA was found to be invariant across parents of children with CCN and parents without children with CCN, a few considerations should be taken into account when applying the PBA in practice among parents of children with CCN.
First, as the PBA assesses burnout within the parenting domain, it does not specifically describe burnout-related feelings with respect to caregiving.
For parents of children with CCN, these two domains are considered intertwined (Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For parents of children with CCN, these two domains are considered intertwined <ref type="bibr">(Patty, van Meeteren, Willemen, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the questions in the PBA might not fully capture the lived experiences of parental burnout among this group.
Unique and nuanced experiences may remain which are only partially captured by the PBA (Abdoli et al., 2020; Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Unique and nuanced experiences may remain which are only partially captured by the PBA <ref type="bibr">(Abdoli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Patty, van Meeteren, Verdonk, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Adjusted domains could potentially improve the assessment of parental burnout for parents of children with CCN, a question yet to be explored.
Second, some of the granularity was lost as a result of collapsing the response categories.
Taking these points into consideration, the PBA can be useful for policy and program evaluation.

As for clinical practice, this study does not provide clinical evidence for applying the PBA in the clinical practice, such application would require further research, for example, how PBA scores translate to clinical symptoms.

Considering the significantly higher PBA scores among parents of children with CCN, this highlights the disproportionate burden experienced by parents of children with CCN and underscores the need for targeted support interventions and awareness for parental wellbeing among professionals (Rosenbaum, 2026).
text.formatted: Considering the significantly higher PBA scores among parents of children with CCN, this highlights the disproportionate burden experienced by parents of children with CCN and underscores the need for targeted support interventions and awareness for parental wellbeing among professionals <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Rosenbaum, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This is further supported by the finding that group membership was the strongest predictor for parental burnout as opposed to the other sociodemographic correlates.
Together these findings underscore the heightened vulnerability to parental burnout among parents of children with CCN.
Future research should further explore amendable contextual factors in relation to parental burnout in parents of children with CCN and without CCN.
